Interviewer:	I tell you a bit about what we’re doing to begin with, that will help you put it all in perspective. We’re interviewing women engineering students mostly who are going on their work placement next year, you’re not going – so we’re also interviewing people, as you can tell, people that aren’t going on placement as a comparison. But we’re looking at women’s educational experiences and why they decided to study engineering? And the ultimate aim of the project is, after we’ve done all the interviews, to put together a policy document that we’re going to give to the Engineering Council looking at ways to try and retain women in the industry (right) and improve the numbers of women in the industry. So that is the project. I’ll start off by asking you some questions about your background and why you decided to take up engineering. Is it aeronautical you’re doing?

Subject:	It is yeah.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did Maths, physics and computing.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, just – well just a comprehensive school, 

Interviewer:	Not a girls’ school or anything?

Subject:	No, no, mixed sort of schooling then over 2 erm, we didn’t have a sixth form, so I went to a specialist sixth form, near where I live to do ‘A’ levels.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, it depends on what you class as the industry. Aviation in general, yeah, because I’ve got a part time job at [name] Airport, but it’s not really the engineering side of things, it’s more passenger services side of things.

Interviewer:	OK, yeah, that’s fine. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	No er none of them did anything like maths or physics or anything – it’s completely unrelated. My dad’s in – he sort of coaches and my mum works in [retail store].

Interviewer:	OK, when and why then do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	I haven’t the foggiest – I haven’t a clue. I always really enjoyed maths at school and it was something that out of all the subjects, it was something I could do – that and physics, you know, really – I enjoyed it most, more than any other subjects and I could do it as well. And also you know, my main ambition is to be an airline pilot and obviously to do that they look at maths and physics quite heavily so, I knew that if that was what I wanted to do, I needed to be good at maths and physics, which was great because I enjoyed it as well and I was quite good at it, so when it came to choosing A levels, it was quite a natural choice really, to get maths and physics, because I needed them and they were my best subjects anyway. But computing was a bit of a (?) – I don’t know why I chose it because I’m awful at computing (laughter) – really bad.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider doing maths or physics at university then?

Subject:	Yeah, I considered it. I mean I didn’t even want to go to University, to be honest. Once I’d finished my A levels I thought right, that’s it, I’ve had enough of education, I’m gonna apply for a pilot’s sponsorship and away I go – how naïve? Er, but obviously before I couldn’t just sort of leave school and do that, I got a job as a Telecom’s analyst for a year, and then as soon as I started sending out applications – September 11th hit and the whole aviation industry went into a slump and I thought, what on earth am I going to do for the next 4/5 years while it picks up, so I decided to go and do a degree ‘cos you know my family wanted me to do it anyway, but I just – I don’t know why, I just didn’t feel drawn to it (yeah) and the more I decided I was going to back to University, obviously I considered maths and physics and everything but erm I’ve always sort of thought well, if I do go to university, I’ll do aeronautical engineering because it kind of combines everything, whereas if you do sort of maths and physics, it’s just a bit hard core really. I think I get enough of it, whereas with engineering you study such a vast range of modules you sort of – it’s a bit of everything, isn’t it? Something to keep you interested. If you were just doing physics, I mean you’d just get really bored with it, so that’s why I chose it.

Interviewer:	OK, so one of the main things that appeals to you about the engineering would be variety?

Subject:	Absolutely, yeah, yeah, I mean whereas this is – if you like for instance maths, you know you’re just doing maths. Or, if you’re doing biology, you’re doing biology, whereas engineering there’s just so many different sub – even in something as specialist as aeronautical engineering, you’re looking at everything related to aircraft but there’s so many different things to look at, you know. So many different modules and you know, we do get a maths module and you know we do some really hard core physics modules and – but you know, 

Interviewer:	But not all the time?

Subject:	Yeah, you get quite a bit of variety.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so how did you decide to do aeronautical engineering, rather than something else – another engineering discipline?

Subject:	Yeah, because I wanted to be in the aviation industry anyway, and I just thought it would transfer nicely. I mean even if I didn’t become a pilot I wanted to work in aviation so – whether it be as an engineer or a pilot or whatever – so it kind of transfers over quite nicely.

Interviewer:	What appeals to you about the aviation industry generally?

Subject:	Oh God, I don’t know. I was like try all of this – from the first time I went on holiday with my family and I just found it completely fascinating, sort of about aircraft and how it works you know, and how something that big will get off the ground, and I just really wanted to be a pilot but I can’t explain it really. It’s so fascinating.

Interviewer:	So did you have much careers advice or anything like that at school?

Subject:	Not really, obviously I had – there was a Careers Officer, we all had those sort of Career interviews in year 10 or whatever. And, it’s all – it sort of gives you a rough idea, you know, you say oh I want to be a pilot or whatever – well go and study computers and maths and physics – right, thanks, bye. It wasn’t – obviously it wasn’t anything too detailed because everyone, you know, you can imagine how many people they’re interviewing and you know, the vast sort of areas they need to go into. But, erm, yeah that was – in high school that was the extent of the careers advice I was given, but when I went to sixth form, I was sort of – I didn’t really know whether I wanted to go to University or not, so I had arranged for another careers interview and he was really good actually. He said, you know, if you did go to University, looking at the subjects you do, you’d probably want to do aeronautical engineering – this is what it entails. Here are the universities that are the best for it, you know, he went into quite a bit of detail, it was quite good.

Interviewer:	Quite supportive?

Subject:	Yeah, absolutely. 

Interviewer:	So did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from doing engineering?

Subject:	Er, I knew quite a few people who’d done like aeronautical engineering particularly, who’d gone through it all beforehand and er they were nothing but supportive. The only thing they did say was you know, just be aware of what you’re letting yourself in for, because it is really, really hard – hard work, lots of work, erm but no, I don’t think I received any discouragement from anyone.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

Subject:	Because when I went for my careers interview, at sixth form, the man said oh [this university’s] the best aeronautical engineering. And then also my dad’s head office is in [university town] so he comes over here quite a lot and also it was – and my best friend’s at [near by] University, so for a number of reasons it was handy. And then, when I came to look around, you know, the department – they were really good and obviously, they had a big aeroplane in there and it all was quite professional and the campus was nice and everything.

Interviewer:	OK, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Oh yeah, yeah, I never had any kind of – because when I took maths and physics at sixth form, it was you know, just me and the boys. So I didn’t think there’d be any girls actually. In fact I thought I might be the only girl doing aeronautical engineering but there’s about 9 of us, at the moment, so there’s been a few more girls than on my other course.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Well not really, because I think – I think the whole maths and physics thing is – I think it’s kind of to do with the way your brain works. Males tend to be better at that kind of thing anyway, so I just think it’s like – and obviously you get couple of females who are really good at it as well and I think it’s the natural way of doing things like – you’ll go into the English, go into the English lecture rooms it’s full of girls – a couple of lads in there. I think it’s just the way it works. I mean, you know ….

Interviewer:	Are there any particular reasons why you think boys are better at maths and science and stuff, than girls?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know actually. I guess, from an early age they’re bought Meccano sets really, aren’t they and girls are encouraged to go off and play with their Barbie, but I think it’s a lot to do with the way your sort of mind works, and if you’re that way inclined, you’ll find a way to do it – nothing’s going to discourage you if it’s what you enjoy. But I think it’s pointless encouraging girls to go into engineering if you know, they’re just not interested in it, which makes them go into engineering anyway.

Interviewer:	So do you think that one of the reasons that there might not be more women, it’s not just because it isn’t what they would like but because they don’t know really what it’s about?

Subject:	Well to be honest, before I came, I really didn’t – I wasn’t that clued about what engineering was about, I knew it was a lot of maths and a lot of physics, so I knew I’d get on with it but I didn’t really understand what it was erm other than when we were at sixth form we went around erm Lancaster University, just to try and get a taste of what was going on. And I went to a talk erm – an engineering talk and you know, I think a lot of people thought engineering was about sort of here, have a spanner and getting greasy and covered in oil and stuff, but that’s a completely different kind of engineer. But I didn’t really know the ins and outs of it. But I think – I think people, when you get to a kind of age when you’re doing you’re A levels, and you’ve shown an interest in maths and physics, I think when it comes to choosing a degree, I think everybody knows that engineering have got to do maths and physics. You know, if you don’t fancy studying maths in great detail or physics in great detail, it’s you know, it’s a bit of both. But I’ve got to be honest, I didn’t really know what it entailed when I came here.

Interviewer:	So is it fair to say it’s not just about knowing what engineering is but it’s even earlier than that if girls just generally don’t decide to do maths and physics, if they don’t do that then they’re not going to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, absolutely because I don’t think – I just think it’s the difference between males – partly the difference between males and females, you know – males tend to go for that, which is why – I don’t know whether that starts in childhood when the boy gets a lego kit and the girl gets a Barbie or what, because I used to play with my brother’s Meccano all the time when I was little. But I just think that’s the way it is.

Interviewer:	OK. What characteristics then do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, somebody calm, unflustered, able to look at a situation and sort of – to take a step back and just sort of think about it logically – you’ve got to have a lot of logic and a lot of common sense. Erm, obviously you’ve got to be good at maths and physics, you’ve got to sort of – when you get a big problem you’ve got to be able to sort of compartmentalise it and look at each problem. Erm, yeah, I think you’ve got to be sort of – just logical about it. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that being logical is seen more as something that men are good at rather than women?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I really don’t know. I guess yes, yeah I’d say yeah actually, ‘cos I think – I don’t know, you’re never gonna escape the fact that most women you know, obviously there are a lot of career women these days but I think you’re still gonna that went around an obstruction that sat in between two loading plates, so we had to design all that and everything. It’s not really a large groups, I’d say just in groups of – anything from 3 to about 7.

Interviewer:	And how do you choose who you want to work with when you’re in a…?

Subject:	Well, in the past it’s been done – it’s been pre-assigned, so you know, you don’t get to work with your friends but this last one, I got to sort of choose the people I was working with, you know.

Interviewer:	Do you find that you prefer to work with women or …?

Subject:	I did work with 2 women actually when I got to choose who I worked with, erm but in the past I’ve been in groups like – no, it doesn’t – it makes absolutely no difference to me, whatsoever.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, occasionally you get like over erm – at the end of the 1st year we had to stay behind for a week, to make a glider out of balsa wood and you had to design it all and everything and there was this one guy in the group and er he had a (?) really bad, like I didn’t know what he was talking about but he felt the need to dominate the group into just his ideas and everyone was sort of saying you know, we will do this kind of thing. And he had no idea of what he was talking about – it was really hard trying to say calm down, no. (laughter) But erm…

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s more of a male thing to be (?) than one of the females?

Subject:	No, no I don’t because I know a girl in er in my year who can be quite sort of domineering. I’ve never worked in a group with her but I can imagine her kind of dominating things sort of, so – but you’re gonna get that whatever. You’re always gonna get someone domineering…

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think that group work helps you in that way?

Subject:	Absolutely, I think it – well, ‘cos when you go into industry that’s what you’re gonna be doing, it’s gonna be sort of mostly team work all the way. So, it’s good that you get to grips with it now and obviously if you’ve got somebody who’s dominating the group or whatever, you’ve got to find a different way of doing what you want to do and it sort of develops, your sort of listening skills and communication skills and that sort of thing. I think it’s essential.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide not to go on placement?

Subject:	I was get a lot of women who are – I mean how many households do you have where the woman’s the bread winner? It’s always the man with the high flying job isn’t it? You’re never gonna get away from that stereotype because it’s actually true that the women are always gonna be lesser earners and erm, their housewives – the woman left at home to bring up the children because they’re not – you know – they can’t go for the managerial positions and earn the same stuff that the man’s earning.

Interviewer:	Do you feel that they should be?

Subject:	Absolutely, there’s absolutely no reason why that shouldn’t happen but erm it’s a funny situation, you know, I think of myself as quite career minded – I’m really ambitious, I’ve known what I wanted to do from an early age and I know it’s not out of my reach. But, my partner’s 8 years older than me and he’s in industry and erm you know we plan to sort of get married next year and everything and he wants a family, obviously, and er and because he’s obviously earning a lot more than me, even though I can leave university and go into industry, he’s still going to be earning that much more than me because he’s been doing it for that much longer. So it is gonna be me, leaving work and bringing up the family, even though I’m just as capable as he is of climbing the ladder and getting into all that stuff. It’s gonna be – he can’t – he can’t really sort of abandon his well paid job and let me sort of bring in a measley wage or whatever, so it’s a bit awkward really, because I’d like to get out there and get on with my career but I’d like a family as well, and that’s the only way to do it. So I think a lot of women are trapped in that kind of cycle, because obviously women to pair up with men who are a lot older than them – well not a lot but about 5 years older than them anyway. So, you know, that’s probably why they’re earning more because they’ve had like a few years more in industry so…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Er, well everyone knows my name so, you know – ‘cos you’re a woman you sort of stand out a little bit more. Other than that, I really don’t know – I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good thing that everyone knows who you are?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d say so, I’d say so. Er, I think another good advantage is in er, in industry they’ve got to employ a certain percentage of women anyway, particularly – yeah, and what I want to do as a pilot, I know that – because, merely because I’m a women I’ve got a better chance than Joe Bloggs next to me who has exactly the same qualifications, simply because they got to employ a certain percentage of women. So you know, it’s not really anything to do with me being better than him, it’s just that I’m a woman. So thats an advantage? 

Interviewer:	Even though it’s an advantage, does it bother you at all?

Subject:	No, it really doesn’t. No, I mean I’m – I’m not bothered by it at all. I’m not bothered that, I stand out more because I’m the minority, it’s just the way it is. 

Interviewer:	Does it bother you that they might be choosing you because you’re a woman and not really because they think you can do the job? Or do you think that would be the case?

Subject:	Oooh, I don’t know – I don’t think that would be the case. I honestly don’t think erm anyone would employ me on the basis that I was a woman. I think I have more chance of – what I’m talking about is if there was me up against a guy with exactly the same subjects and qualifications, I think I’d have more chance, because you know, they’ve got to employ so many women. I don’t think they’d honestly employ me if they didn’t think I was up to the job. Even if he had like a slight cutting edge some way – Ok, fair enough they might employ me, but I don’t think they’d employ me if they didn’t think I was up to the job (yeah). I don’t think that would ever happen.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any particular disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Er, not – well not that I’ve come across personally, no. I think er – no, I just get treated the same as everyone else really – although, there have been a couple of occasions with certain lecturers, who will remain nameless that I’m there, they just look at you as quite (?) I remember once when I was in the first year we did quite a lot of manufacturing, erm practices – and we had to do some work on waves and because there were only 4 waves, we just went in groups of 4 and it was me and 3 lads, and er the guy taking the session spent the whole time watching me on my wave, you know, with me – like I couldn’t hack it, you know. Thinking the machine was too much for me, and the guy next door to me was having like serious problems and it happened sort of like fairly liquid mixture and it was just seeping out of his machine and he was just – (he wouldn’t leave me alone?) and it ‘s just – and you know, other incidences like it where it’s not the people you’re really, really on the degree with, it tends to be the lecturers who kind of, you know, women engineering, whatever next, kind of thing. The older ones mainly. There’s only a little bit of that, though you know, it’s not every lecturer, just a couple.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yes, yeah, one, one.

Interviewer:	Do they treat you differently to the male lecturers, would you say?

Subject:	Erm, no because I really haven’t had – I haven’t spoken to her one on one or anything and I’ve never had any sort of work sessions with her. Erm, so I really wouldn’t know without having – sort of having like a one to one with her or something, so I shouldn’t – there shouldn’t be.

Interviewer:	Do you find it encouraging that you’ve got a female lecturer, would you like to see more female lecturers or aren’t you bothered?

Subject:	Yeah, actually, it would be really nice to see more female lecturers. I don’t know why it’s just sort of girl power (laughter) Yeah, absolutely, yeah, I think it would be good. It would be nice. It would be encouraging actually, yeah. You know she’s made it in a world – a male dominated world, there’s hope for us yet.

Interviewer:	So, has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yeah, actually, it’s been really interesting. Erm, it’s a bit less to do with aircraft than I thought. At the moment it really is quite a lot of physics and everything and er every once in a while they flash us an aeroplane just hoping and thinking (laughter) kind of thing. But yeah, yeah, it’s interesting. It’s exactly what I though it was – a mixture of maths and physics and – it’s hard – it’s hard work, which I knew it would be hard work and it’s very hour intensive erm but it’s nothing that – you know – it’s everything I thought it would be anyway.

Interviewer:	What would you say are the best and the worst things about it?

Subject:	Erm, the best things is – I don’t know, the people you meet. They’re all kind of like minded – everyone does the same thing, there’s a real kind of er – because it’s such a difficult degree there’s a kind of – everybody helps each other, like when we’ve got a really tough piece of course work and everyone’s in there, the day before the deadline, the people who’ve done it, will come over and help out the people who haven’t kind of thing. So you know, it’s a really nice kind of spirit amongst everyone but the down side is just the work load really. We had like 25 hours a week – last semester, which, when you think about when people work they’re doing like 40 hour week, it isn’t very much, but when you think about how much work you’ve got to do in your free time and how tough that work is and how varied it is and in every single module it’s really difficult, that’s quite hard. (Yeah) Interesting though.

Interviewer:	Although the work load may seem a bit unfair, in comparison to people doing say social sciences and stuff like (laughter) (yeah) does it prepare you more for the workplace?

Subject:	Well, yeah, I guess so but – yeah, I guess any sort of engineering you go into, is going to be pretty high stress, lots of work going on, lots of deadlines to meet. Erm, yeah – yeah, I’d say yes. (OK) It can’t be any harder. (laughter)

Interviewer:	Have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah, quite a bit. Erm, we’ve just done a structural design project – we had to design like a framework originally going for a placement actually. Er, and well lots of reasons really. I mean well my partner has quite a few connections in [company] and he’s – he was an engineer for 3 years when he left Uni – he’s still an engineer now, because he did the same degree as me and then he worked at [place] for 3 years, as like a manual engineer, so he knows that side of it as well. But he’s a pilot now but he still does a lot of engineering on the side so he’s got – he works like on a couple of the aircraft of some [company] managers – so he knows them quite well and er he said to them you know, well – ‘cos I know them as well and he said Jenny’s doing Aeronautical Engineering and I wonder if I could abuse the network and get her an interview kind of thing. And both of them have said, oh you know, oh I know this guy here and he owes me a favour, I know that guy there, as long as she gets a decent degree it shouldn’t be a problem. At the end of the day, the only reason why I’d thought an industrial placement would have been of any value, is for my CV – to improve my employability aspect for working at my degree, but I don’t need that. Which sounds really arrogant but I’ve kind of got these contacts but even if that fell through, I still believe that I could – you know – that if I got an interview, that I could still sort of get my way in there. I don’t believe I need t o take an entire year out just to have this diploma in industry on my CV, purely for one section of employability. I mean the idea would’ve been to have the year out and whether I had the year out, they would probably turn round at the end, had I performed well and said, you know, once you’ve done your degree do you fancy coming back? But I don’t think I need it. That sounds really arrogant but – er, I just though it’s a year out and it’s just a year of – a year I don’t need to waste – I’ve already had a year out in industry, so I’ve been in the real world, I know what it’s about, I’ve worked with – you know – people of all ages. I’ve had to – I mean I’ve been in part time work since I was 13, I don’t really feel the need to spend another year out of my education, working.

Interviewer:	Do you think if you hadn’t had a year out, after A levels, you might have thought about it?

Subject:	Er, if I was in the same situation as I am now, probably not, because you know, like I say, even if I hadn’t had the year out – which was brilliant because it was like an office environment, I was working obviously with a team as well. And it was working with people of all ages, all backgrounds and it was invaluable it really was, but I’ve still been, constantly, in part time work since the age of 13 and I think I’ve – even if I hadn’t had the year out, I’d still have really valuable sort of time out in all sorts of places – really diverse places of work, and I’ve met loads of people and you know, obviously I’ve got these sort of contacts here and there and you know, it’s an entire year, which is a long time to improve my employability by a tiny bit really.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any other advantages or disadvantages of the placement?

Subject:	Well really because like – I think if you get a placement with [company], the way I understand it is, they sort of move you about, so once every 2 months you get to spend time in a different department, which is really good because it will give you a better idea of where you – which department – which particular part of aeronautical engineering you really want to go into when you work. But, er I mean that would be invaluable but other than that I can’t really think of anything that would benefit me personally. But other people, who haven’t been out in the workplace, or haven’t had that much experience in working in diverse places with lots of people, would, it would be an invaluable experience.

Interviewer:	Has anyone tried to talk you into going on a placement?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the educational experience and the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s really like in the industry?

Subject:	Ha, that’s a bit of a weird one. 

Interviewer:	What about like gender proportions, the way you’re treated – do you think that’s reflected in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I’ve never worked in engineering industry – I’ve never worked in an industry where it has been male dominated, so I guess I couldn’t really say but I’m – I think er – I’ve got a friend who’s in the Air Squadron and I know she wants to be in the RAF and a couple of – she wanted to be a pilot in the RAF actually, but a couple – she received a bit of negativity from the old boys who were the really old and (?) and think oh, women pilots, what’s going on? But I guess, you know, I’m sure it’s not like that at all because obviously it’s not all old people is it? I just – I think it’ll be fine.

Interviewer:	Do you know what type of company you’d like to go and work for when you finish?

Subject:	Yes, somewhere like [company], erm you know. Somebody who has their finger in all the pies, so you know, they’ve got so many different departments you couldn’t be – like [company] – wonderful company, excellent reputation but it’s all jet engines, but if you wanted to sort of look at air flows and wings and stuff or if you wanted to design fuselages or whatever, that kind of thing, you wouldn’t get the opportunity working in a place that specialises in jet engines. [Company] do so much, you know, you could probably have a kind of – a good choice of where you wanted to work.

Interviewer:	Do you like the idea of being able to move round departments?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah I do. I like the idea of not being pigeon holed to early I like the idea of sort of trying a bit of this and then maybe moving on to a bit of that, after a while and just sort of seeing where I fit in really.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything else that you think attracts you to a company – when you start to look for a job do you think you’ll look at things like at training opportunities?

Subject:	Er, no, not so much training opportunities, that wouldn’t really bother me because I think I’ve had you know, I’ve learnt a lot here and I don’t think they’d put you in charge of anything really important without giving me training or anything. Erm, I don’t – I think Equal Opportunities are getting less and less of an issue these days – personally, although there are some industries where there is a gap between male and females doing the same job – earning different pay, kind of thing. But erm, it – to be honest it wouldn’t really attract me to a company, it would be what areas they specialise in, erm location, salary, salary (laughter) – that’s quite a big pull.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at University?

Subject:	Oh big time because part of being at university is about like the social life and the people you meet and everybody you meet, apart from the lecturers, are in exactly the same boat as you. Everybody’s learning, everybody’s struggling on the same things whereas when you get out into industry, more than likely others – there’ll be a couple of other sort of post graduates fumbling around, but most of the people you meet are gonna be quite experienced engineers and they’re all gonna have their projects to do and I think it’s gonna be – obviously, I’m sure there’ll be places you can go for help and everything, but it’s going to be quite daunting I think. I think you’re gonna – I think I’d really feel the extra responsibility, when I go out into work because I’d be a lot more out on my own and I think it’ll be quite scary.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of skills do you think that you’ll take from the course to work?

Subject:	Erm, what aside from the stuff I learn on the degree?

Interviewer:	Well, both really? Do you think that you will have a chance to put all the theory into practice?

Subject:	Not all of it, not all of it. I’m sure there’ll be some stuff that I never look at ever again but on the other hand if I went to work for somebody like [company] or you know, have to work (??) is an example, er, certainly especially you know the aerodynamic – the core aerodynamic stuff that I’ve learnt, for sure, but all – I think it’s yeah, it’s developed me as a person, it’s helped my communication skills and that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

Subject:	Well the best thing would be erm – I don’t know, I guess you get quite a feeling of accomplishment, putting what you’ve learnt into practice and making a really good job of it. That’d be good. The worst thing would be not having many people in a common position that you can go to and sort of share a problem with because, like I said a lot of people will just be that much more experienced and you’ll be expected just to get on with it and you know, I hate to – I’d hate to be in a place where, you know, it’s just me and everybody else is like middle aged and I think, you know – I know it’s quite a daunting thought, you know, being – I guess loneliness really is how you could describe it – being different to everybody else there – whether that’s by a big age gap or…

Interviewer:	Was that an attraction of a bigger company then, that might take on more graduates?

Subject:	Absolutely –absolutely, definitely, yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the course and the university experience, does generally prepare you for going to work?

Subject:	Erm, well with the work that you do, obviously they give you all the skills that you’re going to need to carry you on into industry, but another thing – they do a lot of teamwork exercises, so that kind of stuff would be really useful but when it comes to dealing with – you know, such a vast range of people, I don’t know – I don’t – I think, I couldn’t say because…

Interviewer:	Do you think it should prepare you or that there is anything else they could do to prepare you when you’re at university?

Subject:	Erm, I mean there probably is. I mean I’ve walked round campus and I’ve seen sort of posters up for like you know, improve your interview skills and stuff like that, which is great ‘cos it means you know, they’re doing quite a lot to help you. But in the department sense it’s just like this is what you need to know and that’s where it finishes. It’s not really the departments anyway but I think for a lot of people it’s gonna come as a shock ‘cos they’re so used to living this life here, going out 3 times a week with their mates and I just think it’s gonna become a big shock when they have to move to a part of the country on their own, set up life with all the responsibility that comes with it, a job in industry. I don’t think anything will prepare you for that really, it’s a life change at the end of the day, isn’t it?

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s anything that makes going into engineering industry, any different from going out and getting any other sort of job?

Subject:	Erm, I think there’s a lot of responsibility that – well there’s a lot of responsibility in loads of jobs, but when it comes to engineering, you know, we design – erm, I’m thinking in an aeronautical sense here but you’re designing parts of aircraft and you know, it’s got to be right. So obviously there’s a lot of responsibility that comes with that. Erm, but er when you say other jobs do you mean like not in engineering just…?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	I don’t know really. I’ve never really thought about it.

Interviewer:	I suppose what I’m thinking is in terms of like the fact that it is so male dominated and that side of the culture that probably isn’t in other spheres.

Subject:	Well yeah, but I think if you do go into engineering anyway, you’re used to that male dominated culture because you’re so (?) using it. So.

Interviewer:	Yeah, Ok. In terms of your career where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Hopefully, you know, in er anything sort of big engineering company doing aeronautical engineering. Or something to do with aeronautics and that kind of thing – hopefully.

Interviewer:	What about in 10 years time?

Subject:	Er, in 10 years time I’d love to be training for my air transport pilot’s licence and making some headway with that ‘cos ultimately that’s where I wanna be and at the end of the day, I’m interested in engineering but it’s not what I want my career – I don’t want to make my career out of it, I just want to get the money – only because it’s £60,000 for an ATPL, which is a lot of years working. And, obviously engineering it’s not that bad these days, so really – it’s sad really but I think it’s a means to an end really but I am interested in it but I don’t – it’s not where I want to spend my career.

Interviewer:	Can you get sponsored to do the pilot’s…?

Subject:	The unfortunate thing is, it used to be almost abundant but it’s a bit rarer these days. In – even the places that do sponsorship, it’s more partial sponsorship where you pay £15,000 up front and there’s like a kind of bond with the airline and they’ll pay the rest and it’s quite complicated.

Interviewer:	Apart from money then, do you think that you’ll have any other difficulties in achieving that aim?

Subject:	Er. Yes. I think the whole thing sort of bringing up a family thing will definitely get in the way because you know, without a doubt I’d be the one taking 5 years out of my life to raise children. You know, I feel I want a family but you know, I want a career as well and I don’t want to spend too much time chained to the house kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s more of a conflict between family and career because of the type of career that you’re doing?

Subject:	Oh absolutely.

Interviewer:	Because it would involve quite a bit of travelling and…?

Subject:	Well yeah, different hours and shift work and erratic hours, night stops, yeah it is a big – a big sort of conflict for family life really, especially if your partners doing exactly the same. Yeah, big style. I mean we’ve still got to work that out really. I think my partner really wants to go into the engineering side and he’s doing his – he’s gonna become like a [?] licensed engineer, so I think he’ll go down that road eventually but erm yeah, yeah, well I think whatever you do I think if you’re a woman then you’ve more than likely got the – you’ve got to do the family thing really and you’ve got to be prepared take time out to do that, which is a big barrier and it always will be as far as I’m concerned. I can’t really see any way around it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, yeah. Yeah I’d say so. I mean it’s a really – a really sort of vast area and I don’t know anything about the structure – how it works at [company] or engineering industries in general, but I should imagine so. I mean I think engineers are pretty well paid and I think that they start off their post graduates at you know about 25 maybe if you’re lucky. But I think it goes up quite high, so I’d say yeah. I mean I think it probably goes up from like a member of the team, project manager, manager and you know, things like that. So yeah I’d say so, I’d say so.

Interviewer:	Are you interested in going into the management side of things or would you like to become more specialised?

Subject:	I think the more – the higher up in a company you become and you know, the more paperwork’s involved and it’s – I’m sure it comes to the stage where you just spend all your time doing paperwork, so that’s not what I want. I’d much rather be on the shop floor with everyone doing the engineering thing, but, you know, I wouldn’t rule it out altogether. Certainly, a much lower grade manager who’d have control of what was going on but would also dig in as well. That kind of thing I’d be up for.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	No, I don’t think I would. Yeah, I ‘m quite happy I mean I don’t regret anything. I still know where I want to go and where I want to be and everything I’m doing now is aiming towards that. I don’t really think I’ve put myself behind – I mean obviously I took a year out but I don’t see it as a drawback at all.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Ooh, er serious, erm, hardworking, daunting, responsible – hmmm, can I pass on a few?

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is masculine?

Subject:	Yeah, without a doubt, without a doubt – yeah.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is? Is it just because there are so many men in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah – yeah, I think that’s the reason. It’s a – I just think it’s the way men are inclined. They’re sort of – they’re just sort of (lets go build stuff?) sort of thing. You know, I think it’s always gonna be like that.

Interviewer:	Do you, do you think that’s …?

Subject:	I don’t think, for a moment, that they’ll ever, in a million years, be as many women in engineering as men.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	Because I don’t think women are that way inclined. I think, you know, if I’d gone for the English degree, it’s all women because that’s the way women’s minds work. Go to the Art classes, it’s all women, it’s just the way their minds work. I think they’re more into the more expressive subjects whereas men – actually it’s a difference – some things are different between men and women – I just think that that’s the way it works and that’s the way it will always be. I don’t – I can’t – I don’t think you’re gonna encourage you know, women to leave that behind. To leave their – you know who they are fundamentally, behind and go and do engineering.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspects of that will cause any problems for you career wise?

Subject:	I don’t know, I think – everybody I’ve met has been incredibly supportive about you know, what I want to do and everything. And I’ve met maybe a couple of people who’ve been like well, you know, you’ve got a tough time ahead of you – good luck kind of thing. Most of the time everyone’s been just incredibly supportive and like erm the place I learnt to fly in, it was just all men, all middle aged – they were all quite old, but they were nothing but supportive of what I wanted to do and everybody’s been like that really so I can’t see they’ll be any problem.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s it thank you very much, that was very helpful.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God, I don’t know. It’s so fascinating.

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Quite supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s good. How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, yeah, I never had any kind of – because when I took maths and physics at sixth form, it was you know, just me and the boys. So I didn’t think there’d be any girls actually. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.text: Well not really, because I think – I think the whole maths and physics thing is – I think it’s kind of to do with the way your brain works. I think it’s just the way it works. I mean, you know ….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there any particular reasons why you think boys are better at maths and science and stuff, than girls?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know actually. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that one of the reasons that there might not be more women, it’s not just because it isn’t what they would like but because they don’t know really what it’s about?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So is it fair to say it’s not just about knowing what engineering is but it’s even earlier than that if girls just generally don’t decide to do maths and physics, if they don’t do that then they’re not going to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely because I don’t think – I just think it’s the difference between males – partly the difference between males and females, you know – males tend to go for that, which is why – I don’t know whether that starts in childhood when the boy gets a lego kit and the girl gets a Barbie or what, because I used to play with my brother’s Meccano all the time when I was little. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What characteristics then do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, somebody calm, unflustered, able to look at a situation and sort of – to take a step back and just sort of think about it logically – you’ve got to have a lot of logic and a lot of common sense. Erm, obviously you’ve got to be good at maths and physics, you’ve got to sort of – when you get a big problem you’ve got to be able to sort of compartmentalise it and look at each problem. Erm, yeah, I think you’ve got to be sort of – just logical about it. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that being logical is seen more as something that men are good at rather than women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. I really don’t know. I guess yes, yeah I’d say yeah actually, ‘cos I think – I don’t know, you’re never gonna escape the fact that most women you know, obviously there are a lot of career women these days but I think you’re still gonna that went around an obstruction that sat in between two loading plates, so we had to design all that and everything. turns.text: And how do you choose who you want to work with when you’re in a…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that you prefer to work with women or …?

turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.text: Do you think that’s more of a male thing to be (?) than one of the females?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think that group work helps you in that way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Absolutely, I think it – well, ‘cos when you go into industry that’s what you’re gonna be doing, it’s gonna be sort of mostly team work all the way. turns.text: OK, why did you decide not to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel that they should be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Absolutely, there’s absolutely no reason why that shouldn’t happen but erm it’s a funny situation, you know, I think of myself as quite career minded – I’m really ambitious, I’ve known what I wanted to do from an early age and I know it’s not out of my reach. It’s gonna be – he can’t – he can’t really sort of abandon his well paid job and let me sort of bring in a measley wage or whatever, so it’s a bit awkward really, because I’d like to get out there and get on with my career but I’d like a family as well, and that’s the only way to do it. So I think a lot of women are trapped in that kind of cycle, because obviously women to pair up with men who are a lot older than them – well not a lot but about 5 years older than them anyway. So, you know, that’s probably why they’re earning more because they’ve had like a few years more in industry so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well everyone knows my name so, you know – ‘cos you’re a woman you sort of stand out a little bit more. Other than that, I really don’t know – I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good thing that everyone knows who you are?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d say so, I’d say so. Er, I think another good advantage is in er, in industry they’ve got to employ a certain percentage of women anyway, particularly – yeah, and what I want to do as a pilot, I know that – because, merely because I’m a women I’ve got a better chance than Joe Bloggs next to me who has exactly the same qualifications, simply because they got to employ a certain percentage of women. So you know, it’s not really anything to do with me being better than him, it’s just that I’m a woman. So thats an advantage?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Even though it’s an advantage, does it bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it really doesn’t. No, I mean I’m – I’m not bothered by it at all. I’m not bothered that, I stand out more because I’m the minority, it’s just the way it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does it bother you that they might be choosing you because you’re a woman and not really because they think you can do the job? Or do you think that would be the case?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oooh, I don’t know – I don’t think that would be the case. I honestly don’t think erm anyone would employ me on the basis that I was a woman. I think I have more chance of – what I’m talking about is if there was me up against a guy with exactly the same subjects and qualifications, I think I’d have more chance, because you know, they’ve got to employ so many women. I don’t think they’d honestly employ me if they didn’t think I was up to the job. Even if he had like a slight cutting edge some way – Ok, fair enough they might employ me, but I don’t think they’d employ me if they didn’t think I was up to the job (yeah). I don’t think that would ever happen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any particular disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not – well not that I’ve come across personally, no. I think er – no, I just get treated the same as everyone else really – although, there have been a couple of occasions with certain lecturers, who will remain nameless that I’m there, they just look at you as quite (?) I remember once when I was in the first year we did quite a lot of manufacturing, erm practices – and we had to do some work on waves and because there were only 4 waves, we just went in groups of 4 and it was me and 3 lads, and er the guy taking the session spent the whole time watching me on my wave, you know, with me – like I couldn’t hack it, you know. Thinking the machine was too much for me, and the guy next door to me was having like serious problems and it happened sort of like fairly liquid mixture and it was just seeping out of his machine and he was just – (he wouldn’t leave me alone?) and it ‘s just – and you know, other incidences like it where it’s not the people you’re really, really on the degree with, it tends to be the lecturers who kind of, you know, women engineering, whatever next, kind of thing. The older ones mainly. There’s only a little bit of that, though you know, it’s not every lecturer, just a couple.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yeah, one, one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do they treat you differently to the male lecturers, would you say?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no because I really haven’t had – I haven’t spoken to her one on one or anything and I’ve never had any sort of work sessions with her. Erm, so I really wouldn’t know without having – sort of having like a one to one with her or something, so I shouldn’t – there shouldn’t be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find it encouraging that you’ve got a female lecturer, would you like to see more female lecturers or aren’t you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, actually, it would be really nice to see more female lecturers. I don’t know why it’s just sort of girl power (laughter) Yeah, absolutely, yeah, I think it would be good. It would be nice. It would be encouraging actually, yeah. You know she’s made it in a world – a male dominated world, there’s hope for us yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, actually, it’s been really interesting. Erm, it’s a bit less to do with aircraft than I thought. At the moment it really is quite a lot of physics and everything and er every once in a while they flash us an aeroplane just hoping and thinking (laughter) kind of thing. But yeah, yeah, it’s interesting. It’s exactly what I though it was – a mixture of maths and physics and – it’s hard – it’s hard work, which I knew it would be hard work and it’s very hour intensive erm but it’s nothing that – you know – it’s everything I thought it would be anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say are the best and the worst things about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best things is – I don’t know, the people you meet. They’re all kind of like minded – everyone does the same thing, there’s a real kind of er – because it’s such a difficult degree there’s a kind of – everybody helps each other, like when we’ve got a really tough piece of course work and everyone’s in there, the day before the deadline, the people who’ve done it, will come over and help out the people who haven’t kind of thing. So you know, it’s a really nice kind of spirit amongst everyone but the down side is just the work load really. We had like 25 hours a week – last semester, which, when you think about when people work they’re doing like 40 hour week, it isn’t very much, but when you think about how much work you’ve got to do in your free time and how tough that work is and how varied it is and in every single module it’s really difficult, that’s quite hard. (Yeah) Interesting though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Although the work load may seem a bit unfair, in comparison to people doing say social sciences and stuff like (laughter) (yeah) does it prepare you more for the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, yeah, I guess so but – yeah, I guess any sort of engineering you go into, is going to be pretty high stress, lots of work going on, lots of deadlines to meet. Erm, yeah – yeah, I’d say yes. (OK) It can’t be any harder. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, quite a bit. Erm, we’ve just done a structural design project – we had to design like a framework originally going for a placement actually. Er, and well lots of reasons really. I mean well my partner has quite a few connections in [company] and he’s – he was an engineer for 3 years when he left Uni – he’s still an engineer now, because he did the same degree as me and then he worked at [place] for 3 years, as like a manual engineer, so he knows that side of it as well. But he’s a pilot now but he still does a lot of engineering on the side so he’s got – he works like on a couple of the aircraft of some [company] managers – so he knows them quite well and er he said to them you know, well – ‘cos I know them as well and he said Jenny’s doing Aeronautical Engineering and I wonder if I could abuse the network and get her an interview kind of thing. And both of them have said, oh you know, oh I know this guy here and he owes me a favour, I know that guy there, as long as she gets a decent degree it shouldn’t be a problem. At the end of the day, the only reason why I’d thought an industrial placement would have been of any value, is for my CV – to improve my employability aspect for working at my degree, but I don’t need that. Which sounds really arrogant but I’ve kind of got these contacts but even if that fell through, I still believe that I could – you know – that if I got an interview, that I could still sort of get my way in there. I don’t believe I need t o take an entire year out just to have this diploma in industry on my CV, purely for one section of employability. I mean the idea would’ve been to have the year out and whether I had the year out, they would probably turn round at the end, had I performed well and said, you know, once you’ve done your degree do you fancy coming back? But I don’t think I need it. That sounds really arrogant but – er, I just though it’s a year out and it’s just a year of – a year I don’t need to waste – I’ve already had a year out in industry, so I’ve been in the real world, I know what it’s about, I’ve worked with – you know – people of all ages. I’ve had to – I mean I’ve been in part time work since I was 13, I don’t really feel the need to spend another year out of my education, working.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think if you hadn’t had a year out, after A levels, you might have thought about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, if I was in the same situation as I am now, probably not, because you know, like I say, even if I hadn’t had the year out – which was brilliant because it was like an office environment, I was working obviously with a team as well. And it was working with people of all ages, all backgrounds and it was invaluable it really was, but I’ve still been, constantly, in part time work since the age of 13 and I think I’ve – even if I hadn’t had the year out, I’d still have really valuable sort of time out in all sorts of places – really diverse places of work, and I’ve met loads of people and you know, obviously I’ve got these sort of contacts here and there and you know, it’s an entire year, which is a long time to improve my employability by a tiny bit really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any other advantages or disadvantages of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well really because like – I think if you get a placement with [company], the way I understand it is, they sort of move you about, so once every 2 months you get to spend time in a different department, which is really good because it will give you a better idea of where you – which department – which particular part of aeronautical engineering you really want to go into when you work. But, er I mean that would be invaluable but other than that I can’t really think of anything that would benefit me personally. But other people, who haven’t been out in the workplace, or haven’t had that much experience in working in diverse places with lots of people, would, it would be an invaluable experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has anyone tried to talk you into going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the educational experience and the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s really like in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ha, that’s a bit of a weird one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about like gender proportions, the way you’re treated – do you think that’s reflected in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’ve never worked in engineering industry – I’ve never worked in an industry where it has been male dominated, so I guess I couldn’t really say but I’m – I think er – I’ve got a friend who’s in the Air Squadron and I know she wants to be in the RAF and a couple of – she wanted to be a pilot in the RAF actually, but a couple – she received a bit of negativity from the old boys who were the really old and (?) and think oh, women pilots, what’s going on? But I guess, you know, I’m sure it’s not like that at all because obviously it’s not all old people is it? I just – I think it’ll be fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what type of company you’d like to go and work for when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, somewhere like [company], erm you know. Somebody who has their finger in all the pies, so you know, they’ve got so many different departments you couldn’t be – like [company] – wonderful company, excellent reputation but it’s all jet engines, but if you wanted to sort of look at air flows and wings and stuff or if you wanted to design fuselages or whatever, that kind of thing, you wouldn’t get the opportunity working in a place that specialises in jet engines. [Company] do so much, you know, you could probably have a kind of – a good choice of where you wanted to work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like the idea of being able to move round departments?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah I do. I like the idea of not being pigeon holed to early I like the idea of sort of trying a bit of this and then maybe moving on to a bit of that, after a while and just sort of seeing where I fit in really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything else that you think attracts you to a company – when you start to look for a job do you think you’ll look at things like at training opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no, not so much training opportunities, that wouldn’t really bother me because I think I’ve had you know, I’ve learnt a lot here and I don’t think they’d put you in charge of anything really important without giving me training or anything. Erm, I don’t – I think Equal Opportunities are getting less and less of an issue these days – personally, although there are some industries where there is a gap between male and females doing the same job – earning different pay, kind of thing. But erm, it – to be honest it wouldn’t really attract me to a company, it would be what areas they specialise in, erm location, salary, salary (laughter) – that’s quite a big pull.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh big time because part of being at university is about like the social life and the people you meet and everybody you meet, apart from the lecturers, are in exactly the same boat as you. Everybody’s learning, everybody’s struggling on the same things whereas when you get out into industry, more than likely others – there’ll be a couple of other sort of post graduates fumbling around, but most of the people you meet are gonna be quite experienced engineers and they’re all gonna have their projects to do and I think it’s gonna be – obviously, I’m sure there’ll be places you can go for help and everything, but it’s going to be quite daunting I think. I think you’re gonna – I think I’d really feel the extra responsibility, when I go out into work because I’d be a lot more out on my own and I think it’ll be quite scary.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of skills do you think that you’ll take from the course to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, what aside from the stuff I learn on the degree?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well, both really? Do you think that you will have a chance to put all the theory into practice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not all of it, not all of it. I’m sure there’ll be some stuff that I never look at ever again but on the other hand if I went to work for somebody like [company] or you know, have to work (??) is an example, er, certainly especially you know the aerodynamic – the core aerodynamic stuff that I’ve learnt, for sure, but all – I think it’s yeah, it’s developed me as a person, it’s helped my communication skills and that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well the best thing would be erm – I don’t know, I guess you get quite a feeling of accomplishment, putting what you’ve learnt into practice and making a really good job of it. That’d be good. The worst thing would be not having many people in a common position that you can go to and sort of share a problem with because, like I said a lot of people will just be that much more experienced and you’ll be expected just to get on with it and you know, I hate to – I’d hate to be in a place where, you know, it’s just me and everybody else is like middle aged and I think, you know – I know it’s quite a daunting thought, you know, being – I guess loneliness really is how you could describe it – being different to everybody else there – whether that’s by a big age gap or…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that an attraction of a bigger company then, that might take on more graduates?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Absolutely –absolutely, definitely, yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the course and the university experience, does generally prepare you for going to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well with the work that you do, obviously they give you all the skills that you’re going to need to carry you on into industry, but another thing – they do a lot of teamwork exercises, so that kind of stuff would be really useful but when it comes to dealing with – you know, such a vast range of people, I don’t know – I don’t – I think, I couldn’t say because…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it should prepare you or that there is anything else they could do to prepare you when you’re at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I mean there probably is. I mean I’ve walked round campus and I’ve seen sort of posters up for like you know, improve your interview skills and stuff like that, which is great ‘cos it means you know, they’re doing quite a lot to help you. But in the department sense it’s just like this is what you need to know and that’s where it finishes. It’s not really the departments anyway but I think for a lot of people it’s gonna come as a shock ‘cos they’re so used to living this life here, going out 3 times a week with their mates and I just think it’s gonna become a big shock when they have to move to a part of the country on their own, set up life with all the responsibility that comes with it, a job in industry. I don’t think anything will prepare you for that really, it’s a life change at the end of the day, isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s anything that makes going into engineering industry, any different from going out and getting any other sort of job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think there’s a lot of responsibility that – well there’s a lot of responsibility in loads of jobs, but when it comes to engineering, you know, we design – erm, I’m thinking in an aeronautical sense here but you’re designing parts of aircraft and you know, it’s got to be right. So obviously there’s a lot of responsibility that comes with that. Erm, but er when you say other jobs do you mean like not in engineering just…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know really. I’ve never really thought about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I suppose what I’m thinking is in terms of like the fact that it is so male dominated and that side of the culture that probably isn’t in other spheres.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well yeah, but I think if you do go into engineering anyway, you’re used to that male dominated culture because you’re so (?) using it. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, Ok. In terms of your career where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, you know, in er anything sort of big engineering company doing aeronautical engineering. Or something to do with aeronautics and that kind of thing – hopefully.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, in 10 years time I’d love to be training for my air transport pilot’s licence and making some headway with that ‘cos ultimately that’s where I wanna be and at the end of the day, I’m interested in engineering but it’s not what I want my career – I don’t want to make my career out of it, I just want to get the money – only because it’s £60,000 for an ATPL, which is a lot of years working. And, obviously engineering it’s not that bad these days, so really – it’s sad really but I think it’s a means to an end really but I am interested in it but I don’t – it’s not where I want to spend my career.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you get sponsored to do the pilot’s…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The unfortunate thing is, it used to be almost abundant but it’s a bit rarer these days. In – even the places that do sponsorship, it’s more partial sponsorship where you pay £15,000 up front and there’s like a kind of bond with the airline and they’ll pay the rest and it’s quite complicated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Apart from money then, do you think that you’ll have any other difficulties in achieving that aim?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er. Yes. I think the whole thing sort of bringing up a family thing will definitely get in the way because you know, without a doubt I’d be the one taking 5 years out of my life to raise children. You know, I feel I want a family but you know, I want a career as well and I don’t want to spend too much time chained to the house kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s more of a conflict between family and career because of the type of career that you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh absolutely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because it would involve quite a bit of travelling and…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well yeah, different hours and shift work and erratic hours, night stops, yeah it is a big – a big sort of conflict for family life really, especially if your partners doing exactly the same. Yeah, big style. I mean we’ve still got to work that out really. I think my partner really wants to go into the engineering side and he’s doing his – he’s gonna become like a [?] licensed engineer, so I think he’ll go down that road eventually but erm yeah, yeah, well I think whatever you do I think if you’re a woman then you’ve more than likely got the – you’ve got to do the family thing really and you’ve got to be prepared take time out to do that, which is a big barrier and it always will be as far as I’m concerned. I can’t really see any way around it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah. Yeah I’d say so. I mean it’s a really – a really sort of vast area and I don’t know anything about the structure – how it works at [company] or engineering industries in general, but I should imagine so. I mean I think engineers are pretty well paid and I think that they start off their post graduates at you know about 25 maybe if you’re lucky. But I think it goes up quite high, so I’d say yeah. I mean I think it probably goes up from like a member of the team, project manager, manager and you know, things like that. So yeah I’d say so, I’d say so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you interested in going into the management side of things or would you like to become more specialised?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the more – the higher up in a company you become and you know, the more paperwork’s involved and it’s – I’m sure it comes to the stage where you just spend all your time doing paperwork, so that’s not what I want. I’d much rather be on the shop floor with everyone doing the engineering thing, but, you know, I wouldn’t rule it out altogether. Certainly, a much lower grade manager who’d have control of what was going on but would also dig in as well. That kind of thing I’d be up for.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think I would. Yeah, I ‘m quite happy I mean I don’t regret anything. I still know where I want to go and where I want to be and everything I’m doing now is aiming towards that. I don’t really think I’ve put myself behind – I mean obviously I took a year out but I don’t see it as a drawback at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh, er serious, erm, hardworking, daunting, responsible – hmmm, can I pass on a few?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, without a doubt, without a doubt – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is? Is it just because there are so many men in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – yeah, I think that’s the reason. It’s a – I just think it’s the way men are inclined. They’re sort of – they’re just sort of (lets go build stuff?) sort of thing. You know, I think it’s always gonna be like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you, do you think that’s …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think, for a moment, that they’ll ever, in a million years, be as many women in engineering as men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because I don’t think women are that way inclined. I think, you know, if I’d gone for the English degree, it’s all women because that’s the way women’s minds work. Go to the Art classes, it’s all women, it’s just the way their minds work. I think they’re more into the more expressive subjects whereas men – actually it’s a difference – some things are different between men and women – I just think that that’s the way it works and that’s the way it will always be. I don’t – I can’t – I don’t think you’re gonna encourage you know, women to leave that behind. To leave their – you know who they are fundamentally, behind and go and do engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any aspects of that will cause any problems for you career wise?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know, I think – everybody I’ve met has been incredibly supportive about you know, what I want to do and everything. And I’ve met maybe a couple of people who’ve been like well, you know, you’ve got a tough time ahead of you – good luck kind of thing. Most of the time everyone’s been just incredibly supportive and like erm the place I learnt to fly in, it was just all men, all middle aged – they were all quite old, but they were nothing but supportive of what I wanted to do and everybody’s been like that really so I can’t see they’ll be any problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s it thank you very much, that was very helpful.
